subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 18 periods = 720 minutes
Total: 18 periods · 12h 0min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Read-Aloud and Poem Exploration

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to share what outdoor games they know, briefly collecting names aloud to build curiosity about the poem's subject.
Teacher reads the poem 'Gilli Danda' aloud expressively, tracking lines on the board or textbook (pp.79–80), pausing at the end of each stanza to let the sound settle.
Teacher reads the poem a second time, inviting students to follow along in their books and tap the rhythm quietly on their desks, noticing rhyming pairs.
Teacher leads a whole-class brief sharing: students name one image or word from the poem that they liked and say why in a single sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the class's first encounter with the poem, so the read-aloud should be unhurried and expressive — modelling the game's energy through pace and stress. The poem's rhyme scheme (round/sound, throw/go, free/see, skies/flies, fun/sun) makes it very accessible for Grade V students, so invite them to notice the rhyming pairs rather than pointing them out first.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the poem's setting — children gathered in a playground with a stick and a gilli — and asks students to open to pp.79–80.
Whole class reads the poem chorally stanza by stanza, with the teacher conducting pace; after each stanza the class identifies the rhyming pair and marks it lightly in pencil.
Students read in two groups alternating stanzas, listening to each other's rhythm and energy; teacher circulates and coaches pronunciation of 'gilli', 'underneath', and 'golden'.
Teacher asks two or three volunteers to read a stanza they enjoyed most and explain in one sentence what image it brings to mind.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who are less confident with reading aloud benefit from the group cover of choral reading before attempting solo lines — the energy of the whole class carries them. Watch for students rushing through the third stanza; the imagery of the gilli flying 'underneath the bright blue skies' deserves a slight pause.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.80): answer questions about the poem's game, feelings, and imagery.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites the class to recall the poem's key images — the gilli flying, bright skies, golden sun — and writes three key words on the board as anchor points.
Teacher poses questions from 'Let us Think — A.' (p.80): which game is described, what equipment is needed, and how the players feel; students discuss in pairs, then share answers with the class.
Teacher continues with questions about what happens when the stick strikes the gilli and which lines show the children are outdoors; students locate evidence in their books and read the lines aloud.

Teacher asks the final two questions — the meaning of 'our game is so sound' and the word in the poem showing happiness — and draws out student reasoning with brief discussion before confirming answers.

periods.teacher_notes: The phrase 'our game is so sound' is the most likely point of confusion; 'sound' here means strong, reliable, or good — not the noise of the game. Encourage students to think of other uses of 'sound' they know (sound advice, sound sleep) before arriving at the poem's meaning. All six questions in 'Let us Think — A.' (p.80) are anchored in this unit.

periods.activity_title: Relating the Poem to Personal Experience and Prior Knowledge

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws students' attention to the poem's refrain 'we never quit' and asks them what they think it means beyond the game itself.
Students discuss in small groups how the poem connects to their own experience of playing outdoors — which details match games they know and which are unfamiliar.
Teacher leads a guided discussion: what traditional games do students know from their families or neighbourhoods, and how do they compare with the poem's description of Gilli Danda?

Students individually write two sentences in their notebooks connecting one image from the poem (gilli flying, golden sun, friends gathering) to a memory of their own outdoor play; two or three share aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's theme of communal, traditional play gives students rich ground to connect to personal knowledge — many may know Gilli Danda from family stories even if they have not played it. Guard against the discussion drifting too far from the poem itself; bring students back to specific lines as anchors.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss — Outdoor Play and Imagination

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.80): discuss outdoor play preferences and imagine the gilli's view.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the discussion with a quick show of hands: who enjoys outdoor games? Who prefers indoor ones? Students note the spread and this becomes the entry point.

Students discuss in pairs the first two questions from 'Let us Think — B.' (p.80): whether they enjoy playing outdoors and why, and naming five outdoor games they play with friends; pairs share their lists with another pair.

Teacher introduces the imaginative prompt from 'Let us Think — B.' (p.80): 'Imagine you are the small gilli — what would you see flying up in the sky?' Students think quietly for a moment, then share with a partner.

Whole-class sharing: four or five students describe what the gilli would see; teacher notes vivid or unexpected images on the board, praising specific detail and helping students extend their descriptions.

periods.teacher_notes: The imaginative prompt — taking the gilli's perspective — is the most demanding of the three questions and should follow the more familiar ones; students who have chanted the poem's third stanza ('The small gilli, up high it flies, / Underneath the bright blue skies') will have richer imagery to draw on. Encourage descriptions grounded in the poem's own images as well as the students' own ideas.

periods.activity_title: Oral Presentation — Describing a Group Game

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (p.80): prepare and deliver a short presentation about a group game.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models a brief oral presentation of a group game using the five-point framework from 'Let us Speak' (p.80) — name, indoor/outdoor, number of players, materials, rules — demonstrating on a familiar game like kabaddi.
Students plan their own presentation individually, jotting five points about a group game of their choice; teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with guiding questions.

Six to eight students deliver their presentations to the class; the audience listens and notes one thing they learned about each game; teacher gives brief oral feedback after each on clarity and detail.
Class compares: which games mentioned were indoor, which outdoor? Teacher charts responses briefly on the board to close the unit with a visual summary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may conflate 'rules' with 'how to win'; guide them to include safety instructions as the task requires — this is particularly relevant for outdoor games with equipment like Gilli Danda. Presentations need not be long; three or four clear sentences covering most of the five points is fully adequate at this stage.

periods.activity_title: Listen and Respond — Action Game with the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.80): listen to teacher cues and respond with matching actions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the listening activity: she will read phrases from the poem aloud and students respond with the matching physical action; demonstrates one example with 'Swing and hit'.

Teacher reads each of the four cue phrases from 'Let us Listen' (p.80) — 'Swing and hit', 'Watch it go!', 'Laughing, playing', 'Shade your eyes from the sun' — at varying speeds and in random order; students perform the matching action each time.
Students work in pairs: one partner calls the phrase, the other responds with the action; partners switch roles after each round, repeating three to four times.

Teacher leads a reflection: students close their eyes while she reads the whole poem aloud slowly, and they perform the appropriate action whenever one of the four cue phrases appears; the class settles with a final choral recitation of the last stanza.

periods.teacher_notes: This kinaesthetic activity helps cement the poem's vocabulary and imagery through embodied response — students who found the text challenging in earlier reading units often engage more successfully here. Watch that the 'Shade your eyes' action is clearly modelled so students do not confuse it with blocking the sun entirely; the hands rest above the eyebrows, mimicking looking into the distance.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.81): add 'un-' or 're-' prefixes and write new words with meanings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces prefixes using the textbook example (p.81): 'unhappy' and 'redo'. She writes 'un = not' and 're = again' on the board and asks students to call out one more word for each.

Teacher works through 'Let us Learn — A.' (p.81) with the class: students say each base word aloud — write, aware, comfortable, arrange, think — decide which prefix fits and why, then write the new word and its meaning in their notebooks.

Pairs compare their answers and discuss one word where both prefixes might seem possible; teacher facilitates a brief whole-class check, clarifying 'rethink' vs 'unthink' and why only one is a real English word.
Students compose one sentence using any two of the five new words; two or three volunteers share their sentences and the class checks that the prefix meaning is correctly reflected.

periods.teacher_notes: The word 'uncomfortable' is straightforward, but 'rewrite' and 'rearrange' are the most useful for students' own writing — draw attention to their practicality. Some students may attempt 'unwrite' or 'unthink'; treat these as opportunities to discuss which prefixes combine naturally with which roots in English rather than as errors.

periods.activity_title: Abstract and Concrete Nouns — Sorting Activity

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (p.82): sort the noun grid into concrete and abstract; generate more abstract nouns.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads two nouns from the poem — 'sun' and 'joy' — and asks: can you see, touch, taste or smell each one? This sensory test establishes the concrete/abstract distinction without technical jargon first.
Students work through the word grid in 'Let us Learn — B.' (p.82) individually, encircling concrete nouns they can see, taste, touch, or smell; they leave abstract nouns unencircled.
Class reviews the grid together; teacher invites students to justify one or two borderline choices (e.g. 'chessboard' is concrete, 'happiness' is abstract); students adjust their answers if needed.
Students think of two or three more abstract nouns from their own experience and share them; teacher lists them on the board and the class confirms each one passes the 'cannot be sensed' test.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often struggle with 'truth' and 'lie' at first glance, treating them as concrete because they are familiar; use the sensory test consistently — can you hold truth in your hand or taste a lie? — to guide reasoning rather than simply stating the answer. The grid task in 'Let us Learn — B.' (p.82) has no question bank in the summary, so no specific question_bank items are anchored here.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.83): fill blanks with correct possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs).

time_bands.activity: Teacher picks up an object — a book or pen — and says 'This belongs to me, so it is mine'; passes it to a student who says 'Now it is yours'; continues briefly to build intuition for each possessive pronoun form before opening the textbook.
Students work through 'Let us Learn — C.' (p.83) independently, reading each sentence carefully to identify whose the object is before choosing from: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.

Teacher reads each sentence aloud and cold-calls students for answers; where an answer is incorrect she repeats the ownership clue in the sentence ('belongs to my cousins — more than one person — so?') to scaffold self-correction.
Students write two original sentences using any two possessive pronouns of their choice and exchange notebooks with a partner to check whether the ownership matches the pronoun used.

periods.teacher_notes: Sentence 3 — 'belongs to my cousins' — trips up students who default to 'ours'; remind them that 'ours' requires the speaker to be included in the group. The Jal Tarang context in sentence 4 may be unfamiliar; briefly explain it is a musical instrument played with water-filled bowls so the sentence makes sense before students answer.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (p.85): find meanings of five poem words and use each in an original sentence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates dictionary use with the word 'gilli' (or a word students know) — locating the entry, reading the definition, and composing a sentence; models how to ensure the sentence shows the word's meaning in context.
Students use dictionaries to look up each of the five words from 'Let us Write — A.' (p.85) — quit, gather, swing, underneath, golden — and write the meaning beside each word in their notebooks.

Students write one original sentence for each word, ensuring the sentence context shows they understand the meaning; teacher circulates and gives brief individual feedback on two or three students' sentences.
Three or four volunteers share one of their sentences; class listens and gives a thumbs-up if the sentence clearly shows the word's meaning, or suggests an improvement if not.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write sentences like 'I quit the game' that technically use the word but do not reveal understanding of its meaning; encourage sentences that show the word in a fuller context, such as 'She quit because she was very tired.' The five words — quit, gather, swing, underneath, golden — all appear in the poem, so students may draw on the poem's own context as a model.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — B. (p.85): rearrange scrambled words to form correct questions.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write — C. (p.85): write three words with each of the double letters tt, pp, ee, mm, bb, rr, nn, dd, ss, gg.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'the are cows where' on the board and asks students what is wrong; elicits that questions need a question word at the start and a question mark at the end, then models the correct rearrangement.

Students work through all eight scrambled items from 'Let us Write — B.' (p.85) in their notebooks, applying the rearrangement rule and adding question marks; teacher moves around the room and prompts students who are uncertain about where the question word belongs.
Teacher writes each scrambled set on the board one by one, invites student answers, and discusses any differing versions — particularly where more than one arrangement sounds grammatical.
Students write one original scrambled question of their own and swap with a partner to rearrange it correctly; partners share results.

periods.teacher_notes: Several of the eight items have a wh-question word that gives the starting point — 'where', 'which', 'what', 'why', 'how', 'when' — so teach students to locate the question word first as a strategy. The homework item on double letters ('Let us Write — C.', p.85) is set here as independent word-play practice; it does not require teacher facilitation to attempt.

periods.activity_title: Antonyms in Context — Circle the Odd Word

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — D. (p.87): circle the word different in meaning from the underlined word.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'expensive' on the board and lists three words beneath: 'precious, costly, cheap'. She asks: two of these mean something similar — which is the odd one out and why? Establishes the antonym-identification task clearly.
Students work through all eight items in 'Let us Write — D.' (p.87) independently, circling the odd word in each set and writing a brief reason beside each answer.
Teacher leads a whole-class review, working through each item; for any item where students chose differently, she invites both sides to explain their reasoning before confirming the answer.
Students choose two of the underlined words from the exercise and write a sentence for each, then swap with a partner who checks that the sentence meaning aligns with the word's sense.

periods.teacher_notes: Item 6 — 'nervously / sadly / joyfully / confidently' — is the most nuanced; both 'joyfully' and 'confidently' differ from 'nervously', but only 'confidently' is the true antonym (opposite manner). Encourage students to test each option against the underlined word rather than stopping at the first word that seems different. All eight items in 'Let us Write — D.' (p.87) are anchored in this unit.

periods.activity_title: Make a Gilli Danda from Waste Material

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (pp.88–89): make a gilli and danda using waste material following the textbook steps.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads through the materials list and steps for making the gilli and danda from 'Let us Do — A.' (pp.88–89) with students, checking that everyone has what they need and clarifying the shaping of the gilli's tapered ends.

Students work in pairs to complete the construction steps — finding and smoothening the sticks, shaping the gilli's ends, and optionally decorating with colours or paper; teacher circulates and assists, ensuring each pair tests that their gilli and danda are sturdy.
Each pair displays their finished gilli and danda; students do a gallery walk, observing other pairs' work and noting one thing they did similarly and one thing differently.
Teacher leads a brief reflection: what was the most difficult step, and what does making the equipment tell us about how the game has been played traditionally without shop-bought gear?

periods.teacher_notes: Students should bring materials from home or the school grounds; the instructions in 'Let us Do — A.' (pp.88–89) specify a thick firm twig for the danda and a shorter stick for the gilli, with a rough stone for smoothening. If outdoor materials are unavailable, thick craft sticks or dowel rods work as substitutes — the pedagogical goal is the making process and the connection to traditional play, not perfect equipment.

periods.activity_title: Spellathon — Word-Making from a Letter Wheel

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Just for Fun — B. (p.90): make three-letter-or-more words from the letter wheel (A, C, E, T, H, E, R).

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the letter wheel from 'Just for Fun — B.' (p.90) on the board — letters A, C, E, T, H, E, R — explains the rules (three or more letters, each letter used only as many times as it appears), and shows two examples: 'tea' and 'reach'.

Students work individually to find as many words of three or more letters as possible, writing them in their notebooks; teacher circulates, nudging students who are stuck with prompts like 'try starting with H' or 'what words end in -er?'

Class pools their words in a list on the board sorted by length; teacher awards a brief cheer for any seven-letter word — the answer is 'teacher' — if no student finds it, the teacher reveals it and the class verifies it uses each letter correctly.
Students create their own letter wheel of seven letters in their notebooks and challenge a partner to find as many words as possible; partners swap notebooks and attempt each other's wheels.

periods.teacher_notes: The seven-letter word hidden in the wheel is 'teacher' — worth celebrating when students find it, as it makes the activity personally resonant. Students often overlook two-syllable words; after they have found single-syllable words, prompt them to think of words that contain two of the vowels (A and E both appear).

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Just for Fun — Riddle (p.90): reason through the riddle and discuss the answer.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the riddle from 'Just for Fun' (p.90) — 'It belongs to you, but your friends use it more than you. What is it?' — allows a full silent minute for students to think before anyone speaks.
Students discuss in pairs, listing two or three possible answers with reasons; teacher circulates without hinting, encouraging pairs to test each guess against both conditions of the riddle.

Whole-class sharing of guesses; teacher writes each on the board and the class tests them with the two-condition test: does it belong to you? Do your friends use it more? Students debate until they arrive at 'your name'.

Students compose their own riddle in two or three sentences using a similar structure ('It belongs to you / It is part of you / others use it more'), then share with a partner who tries to solve it before the author reveals the answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The answer to the riddle is 'your name' — others call it out far more than you say it yourself. Students may initially suggest 'money' or 'toys'; the two-condition test on the board helps them reason past surface answers. Creating their own riddle in the second half deepens the reasoning skill and gives the unit its own complete arc.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud once more as a model of expressive delivery, then invites students to identify one word or phrase in each stanza that carries the most energy and mark it in their books.

Students practise the poem in pairs — each reading alternate stanzas, coaching each other on pace, stress, and expression; teacher moves around the room to give brief feedback on fluency and expression.

Volunteers perform individual or paired recitations of the full poem for the class; classmates listen for clear pronunciation of 'gilli', 'underneath', and 'golden' and applaud after each performance.
Whole class recites the final stanza together as a closing chant, with teacher conducting pace; students close their books and recite as much as they can from memory.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit brings reading fluency and oral performance together on the same text — the expressive delivery students have practised through choral reading in earlier units of this poem finds its fullest expression here. Students who are shy about solo performance should be encouraged but not forced; paired recitation is a valid and equally rich option.

periods.activity_title: Chapter Synthesis — Gilli Danda: Bringing It All Together

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the synthesis with a whole-class map: she draws five branches on the board labelled reading, speaking, listening, words, and beyond — and invites students to name one thing they remember from each, drawing on the poem, the games discussion, the noun sorting, the prefix work, and the Spellathon.

Quick review round: teacher poses one question per strand — one comprehension question about the poem's imagery, one vocabulary question about a prefix word, one grammar question about a possessive pronoun, and one riddle — students respond orally as a class, with no notebooks needed.

Students write a short paragraph (four to five sentences) in their notebooks describing Gilli Danda — what it is, how it is played, why the poem celebrates it, and one word from the chapter that is new to them and that they now understand; the paragraph begins and ends within this unit.
Four or five students share their paragraphs; after each the teacher invites a peer to name one word or phrase the writer used well, building a brief oral celebration of the chapter's vocabulary.
Teacher closes with the final stanza of the poem — 'Laughing, playing, having fun, / Under the golden rays of the sun!' — read in unison as a collective farewell to the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the poem's imagery of communal joy — friends gathering, the gilli flying, golden sunrays — as well as the language work on prefixes, abstract nouns, possessive pronouns, and vocabulary from the poem. Students who have covered different subsets of units in earlier sittings will all share the poem as common ground, so anchoring the synthesis in the poem's content ensures every student has a point of entry.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on Textbook page 79 beginning "The small gilli, up high it flies." Which two details in these lines tell us that the children are playing outside in the open air?

options.label: A
options.text: The bright blue skies and the golden rays of the sun.

options.label: B
options.text: The stick and the small gilli.

options.label: C
options.text: The laughter of the children and the game's rules.

options.label: D
options.text: The number of players and the size of the playground.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student is focusing on the game's equipment rather than the imagery that signals an outdoor setting.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student is drawing on general knowledge about games rather than reading the imagery in this stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is inferring details not present in the poem, missing the specific sky and sun imagery.

items.item_stem: The poem says 'our game is so sound.' In your own words, explain what 'sound' means in this line and how the poem shows that the children feel that way about their game.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: In this line, 'sound' means strong, reliable, or good — the children are saying their game is a great one. The poem shows this through lines like 'we never quit' and the joyful energy of playing together with friends.

items.item_stem:
Listen carefully. Your teacher will say a phrase from the Gilli Danda poem. Decide whether the statement below is TRUE or FALSE.

1. 'Swing and hit' means you pretend to strike an invisible danda.
2. 'Watch it go!' means you sit down and look at the floor.
3. 'Laughing, playing' means you giggle or clap your hands.
4. 'The golden rays of the sun' tells us it is night-time in the poem.

options.text: 'Swing and hit' means you pretend to strike an invisible danda.
'Watch it go!' means you sit down and look at the floor.
'Laughing, playing' means you giggle or clap your hands.
'The golden rays of the sun' tells us it is night-time in the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True (swinging an invisible danda matches 'swing and hit'); 2 — False (the action is raising arms to watch the gilli fly, not looking at the floor); 3 — True (giggling or clapping matches the joyful action); 4 — False (golden rays of the sun indicate daytime, not night).

items.item_stem: The poem imagines children gathering in a playground to play Gilli Danda. Think of a group game you enjoy playing with your friends. In three or four sentences, tell your class: the name of the game, whether it is played indoors or outdoors, how many players are needed, and one rule that makes the game safe and fair.

expected_elements: Names the game and indoor/outdoor setting.
Shares one safety or fairness rule.

items.item_stem:
Fill in each blank with the correct word from the box to complete the sentence. Each word should fit the meaning of the sentence.

Box: gather   quit   underneath   golden   swing

1. The children decided to __________ in the playground before the game began.
2. She would not __________ even when the game became difficult.
3. The gilli flew __________ the bright blue skies.
4. The bat makes a wide __________ before hitting the ball.
5. Warm __________ sunlight filled the field as the children played.

items.item_stem: The poem celebrates playing Gilli Danda with friends and never quitting. Write three sentences about a time you played a game with friends outdoors. Use at least two of these words from the poem in your sentences: gather, swing, golden, underneath, quit.

expected_elements: Uses at least two poem words correctly.
Describes an outdoor play experience clearly.

items.item_stem: Match each base word in Column A with the correct prefix in Column B to make a new word. Then match the new word to its meaning in Column C.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B | Column C
arrange | un- | to do again
comfortable | re- | not at ease
write | re- | to put in order again
aware | un- | to write again
think | un- | not knowing

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: arrange → re- → rearrange (to put in order again); comfortable → un- → uncomfortable (not at ease); write → re- → rewrite (to write again); aware → un- → unaware (not knowing); think → re- → rethink (to think again).

answer_key.right: re- → rearrange: to put in order again

items.item_stem: The poem describes 'joy' and 'fun' — two feelings the children have while playing. Choose ONE of these words: joy, happiness, fear, or anger. Say whether it is a concrete noun or an abstract noun, and then say one sentence aloud explaining how you know.

expected_elements: Correctly identifies the word as abstract noun.
Uses a clear spoken sentence to explain.

items.source_lo: Student engages in hands-on making, word-play puzzles, and riddle reasoning extending the poem's cultural and language themes.
items.source_context: Making gilli-danda from waste material, Spellathon letter wheel (A,C,E,T,H,E,R), riddle about names.
items.item_stem: Match each step on the left with the correct part of making a Gilli Danda on the right.
items.visual_stimulus:
Step | Part of Making
Find a thick, firm twig | Making the danda
Sharpen both ends to a point | Shaping the gilli
Smoothened with a rough stone | Finishing both pieces
Decorate with colours or paper | Optional final touch
Test that it is sturdy and easy to handle | Final check

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Find a thick, firm twig → Making the danda; Sharpen both ends to a point → Shaping the gilli; Smoothened with a rough stone → Finishing both pieces; Decorate with colours or paper → Optional final touch; Test that it is sturdy and easy to handle → Final check.

answer_key.left: Sharpen both ends to a point

items.item_stem: The Spellathon letter wheel in Textbook page 90 contains the letters A, C, E, T, H, E, R. Using only these letters (each letter used only as many times as it appears in the wheel), write down three words of three or more letters that you can make. Then share your three words aloud and explain one of them in a sentence.

expected_elements: Produces three valid words of three-plus letters.
Each word uses only letters from A, C, E, T, H, E, R.
Explains one word clearly in a spoken sentence.
